replying_to: Replying to Block Contextual MDPs for Continual Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper4654 by Reviewer 8QEN

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies continual reinforcement learning setting through the block contextual MDP framework. Contextual MDPs assume a distribution of MDPs such that there is a mapping from a context to the reward and transitions. Block contextual MDPs furtherer assume that the observations are also a function of the context. The theory section gives bounds on the performance of the optimal policy for a new context c2 given a policy that is \epsilon optimal for context c1 and given that c1 is close to c2. The authors then propose a representation learning algorithm that learns a task representation (learns the context) as a function of history via a model based loss function. The experiments compare this method with some baselines in a continual RL setup.
content.main_review:
This papers studies an important problem of non stationarity in RL via the contextual MDP framework. This is a nice idea and there are some nice results in this paper. However, there are many missing parts, questions about some of the assumptions, missing algorithm description and questionable experiments. More work has to be done before it will be ready to published, but there are good results here and I encourage the authors to improve this paper. I hope that my more detailed comments below will help. 

I would like to start from the main claim of this paper: to study non stationarity via contextual MDPs. This is. nice idea, but I would like to see some definitions about it: is there a distribution over contexts? is it changing over time? is it changing in a smooth way? are there "k" abrupt changes? without giving a formal definition for that, it is hard to understand the connection to contextual MDPs, the algorithm, and the empirical setup. For example, what exactly is the proposed approach? to use the policy from previous tasks on a new task assuming that it didn't change much and assuming that it is close to them from continuity? I really can't find a single (or multiple) story in this paper that explains me how the algorithm is dealing with non stationarity and what the theory is saying on that. This is also why I find the experiments confusing but I will add on this later. 

I don't understand Figure 1, and I am missing a discussion about it. What is the difference between the arrows, why is a new context sampled at each time step? if the context is just a state at a different time scale, then maybe the problem that is studied in this paper is more about a factored MDP. 

The literature review section is highly confusing. It is trying to cover too much, too early in the paper, and it cites too many irrelevant papers. It is ok to expand more in the appendix (as the authors have already done) but this section really confuses me. For example, I don't see right away what is the connection between meta RL to contextual MDPs. It might be easier to understand this connection from the experiments that were performed, but at the beginning of the paper I really don't see it. I would much prefer to have the connection explained to me over seeing numerous citations to papers at this point. At the same time, I would like to see much more explanation on the topic of block contextual mdps, which seems to be the topic of this work. In particular, I am missing some literature review on rich observation MDPs (there are many papers on this topic from MSR NYC, e.g., [2],[3],[4]). Finally, I think that a much more detailed discussion on the two papers by Modi. et al would be appropriate, and other papers on contextual MDPs should be at least mentioned (e.g. [5]). 

Theory section. 
The main problem with this section is that it is giving bounds on what would a good context space would give me, while there is no result in this section about how to learn such a context space, which is what the algorithm and the experiments are doing. This was very confusing for me while I was reading the paper. In contrast, in contextual MDPs, the context is usually observed, the agent is learning a mapping from this context to the reward and the transitions, and uses this mapping for zero shot transfer (with PAC or regret results, e.g., in Modi et al.). 

Another high level issue is that all of the results in this section are given for tabular representations, while the paper claims to study block contextual mdps. This is an over claim in this case as the block part extends contextual mdps by introducing a mapping from context to observations, but this mapping (and the observations in general), are never studied. 

Theorem 1 should be a corollary, as it is a straight forward application of the simulation lemma [1].  

Assumption 1 seems to be impractical. The authors should try and give an example for a setup where it might hold. In particular, some assumption about the learning algorithm and/or the data distribution in those k steps that the agent takes, and a variable \delta that measures the probability to identify in k steps. It seems that Defintion 5 and Theorem 3 are going in the direction of defining the data distribution but the discussion was not clear to me. Also note that Theorem 3 is with high probability while Assumption 1 is not. 

Theorem 3: bounding the rewards is loosing generality. That is of course a standard class of rewards in RL, so why state that it is without the loss of generality? 

Theorem 5 is not really a generalization bound, it is more of a transfer bound. What this theorem says essentially is that for tasks that are close to each other, an approximate policy on one task is also an approximate policy on another task, which is again an application of the simulation Lemma. A generalization bound is usually giving us an upper bound on any future context c from some class, after seeing some n contexts from this class. 

Section 5. 
This section is describing the algorithm but is missing a lot of details. Equation 2 is confusing as \phi and \psi were not defined yet. Learning the context from history is not straight forward to me, because the context is usually independent of the experience collected in a task. I would like to see something being said or defined on that, i.e., that such a learning process can actually work in a tabular environment. It is also not clear to me how the policy agent is using the representation. 

Section 6. 
In the experiments section, I am missing a description of the non stationarity setup and how the Zeus algorithm is dealing with non stationarity. If this is the main point in the paper then I would like to understand it exactly. I learn very little from the comparison to the baselines, this seems like an independent contribution. Instead I would like to see some connection to the theory part, and ablations, that explain me what are the important components of the algorithm and how sensitive they are to the non stationarity.  

[1] Kearns, Michael, and Satinder Singh. "Near-optimal reinforcement learning in polynomial time." Machine learning 49.2 (2002): 209-232.

[2] Du, S., Krishnamurthy, A., Jiang, N., Agarwal, A., Dudik, M., & Langford, J. (2019, May). Provably efficient RL with rich observations via latent state decoding. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 1665-1674). PMLR.

[3] Dann, Christoph, Nan Jiang, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Alekh Agarwal, John Langford, and Robert E. Schapire. "On oracle-efficient PAC RL with rich observations." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2018 (2018): 1422-1432.

[4] Jiang, Nan, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Alekh Agarwal, John Langford, and Robert E. Schapire. "Contextual decision processes with low Bellman rank are PAC-learnable." In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 1704-1713. PMLR, 2017.

[5] Belogolovsky, Stav, Philip Korsunsky, Shie Mannor, Chen Tessler, and Tom Zahavy. "Inverse reinforcement learning in contextual MDPs." Machine Learning (2021): 1-40.

content.title: Thank you for your feedback! 1/3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their detailed feedback and are glad that they find "This is a nice idea and there are some nice results in this paper." We address their questions below and look forward to discussing these points with them.

> is there a distribution over contexts?is it changing over time? is it changing in a smooth way? are there "k" abrupt changes?

No, we do not assume a distribution over the contexts. During testing, the agent is evaluated on multiple held out environments (each with a different context) where the context is not accessible to the agent.

> what exactly is the proposed approach? to use the policy from previous tasks on a new task assuming that it didn't change much and assuming that it is close to them from continuity? 

The proposed approach is to perform online inference of the context and use that to guide the agent (by feeding as an input to the policy) to perform the given task.

> really can't find a single (or multiple) story in this paper that explains me how the algorithm is dealing with non stationarity and what the theory is saying on that. 

In the introduction (page 1, last paragraph), we mention "introduce Lipschitz Block Contextual MDP framework that leverages results connecting Lipschitz functions to generalization (Xu & Mannor, 2012) and enables us to frame nonstationarity as a changing context over a family of stationary MDPs (thus modelling it as a contextual MDP). We propose a representation learning algorithm...works by constructing a context space that is Lipschitz with respect to the changes in dynamics and reward of the nonstationary environment". In practice,  it means that we infer the context while ensuring certain Lipschitz properties hold because those Lipschitz properties guarantee generalization to new contexts, or the ability to adapt to new nonstationarity not seen at training time. The main results about generalization properties of Lipschitz BC-MDPS are given in section 5.

> I don't understand Figure 1, and I am missing a discussion about it. What is the difference between the arrows

The dotted arrows show the dependencies involving the context while the solid arrow shows dependencies that do not involve the context. We will add this point in the paper.

> why is a new context sampled at each time step?

The image shows the graphical model for a BC-MDP where the context could (possibly) change per timestep.

> The literature review section is highly confusing. It is trying to cover too much, too early in the paper, and it cites too many irrelevant papers. It is ok to expand more in the appendix (as the authors have already done) but this section really confuses me. For example, I don't see right away what is the connection between meta RL to contextual MDPs.

Our work is related to both contextual MDPs (as first described in the last paragraph on page 1) and meta-RL literature (given the method is inspired from adaptive control), as described on page 2. We will move some parts of the related work to the appendix.

> At the same time, I would like to see much more explanation on the topic of block contextual mdps, which seems to be the topic of this work. In particular, I am missing some literature review on rich observation MDPs (there are many papers on this topic from MSR NYC, e.g., [2],[3],[4]). Finally, I think that a much more detailed discussion on the two papers by Modi. et al would be appropriate, and other papers on contextual MDPs should be at least mentioned (e.g. [5]).

Thank you for the additional references, we will add them to the paper.

> The main problem with this section is that it is giving bounds on what would a good context space would give me, while there is no result in this section about how to learn such a context space, which is what the algorithm and the experiments are doing. 

In the paper, we are providing the motivation for why we want to learn a lipschitz BC-MDP and the algorithm section shows how to do it and how to measure its error to determine generalization capability. While there are tools that would bound the approximation error (for learning a good context space), it relies on much stricter assumptions about the type of algorithm used to explore each MDP and are less tractable in larger problem domains.

> This was very confusing for me while I was reading the paper. In contrast, in contextual MDPs, the context is usually observed, the agent is learning a mapping from this context to the reward and the transitions, and uses this mapping for zero shot transfer (with PAC or regret results, e.g., in Modi et al.).

We agree with the difference the reviewer is pointing out and highlight that assuming access to a well-defined and informative context can be impractical in several setups. Even in the cases where we can assume access to the context during training, the agent may not have access to the context during evaluation (even less likely when the agent is in an unseen environment). In those cases, inferring the context is a key requirement.

> Another high level issue is that all of the results in this section are given for tabular representations, while the paper claims to study block contextual mdps. This is an over claim in this case as the block part extends contextual mdps by introducing a mapping from context to observations, but this mapping (and the observations in general), are never studied.

Performing similar theoretical analysis with neural network components is an open research area. We understand the reviewer's concern about the feasibility of applying these results (obtained for tabular representations) to the more general and complex setting. This is why, along with the theoretical results, we include several experiments to show that the general idea of leveraging the Lipschitz property helps to improve the performance in practice. 

> Theorem 1 should be a corollary, as it is a straight forward application of the simulation lemma [1].

We have incorporated this feedback in the paper.

> Assumption 1 seems to be impractical. The authors should try and give an example for a setup where it might hold. 

Assumption 1 is implicit in all the works that leverage neural networks to infer the context or to identify system parameters. Some examples are mentioned in the related work section and used as baselines. For an example where the assumption might hold, consider the example of a robot operating in different warehouses. In one warehouse, it only observes/interacts with solid objects like metallic cubes and in another warehouse, it only observes/interacts with deformable objects like clothes. In a few interactions, the robot can infer if the objects are solid or deformable.

> Theorem 5 is not really a generalization bound, it is more of a transfer bound.  What this theorem says essentially is that for tasks that are close to each other, an approximate policy on one task is also an approximate policy on another task, which is again an application of the simulation Lemma. A generalization bound is usually giving us an upper bound on any future context c from some class, after seeing some n contexts from this class.

We clarify that in "an approximate policy on one task, s also an approximate policy on another task," the policy is a context conditioned policy and therefore the policy behavior changes when the context encoder infers a new context. We do not "use the policy from previous tasks on a new task assuming that it didn't change much and assuming that it is close to them from continuity?" (as discussed in a previous point above). We highlight this difference to make sure that there is not confusion about this part. 

> Section 5. This section is describing the algorithm but is missing a lot of details.
 
We describe the implementation details, along with pseudo code in the appendix (section B). We will move some of the content to the main paper.

> Equation 2 is confusing as \phi and \psi were not defined yet. 

We apologize for the confusion and will make it more clear in the paper. \psi represents the (learned) context encoder and \phi represents the (learned) dynamics model.

> Learning the context from history is not straight forward to me, because the context is usually independent of the experience collected in a task. I would like to see something being said or defined on that, i.e., that such a learning process can actually work in a tabular environment. 

Consider the example of driving a car where the friction coefficient between the car and the road varies across the tasks. In this case, given the transition history (across different tasks), the system can infer the friction coefficient between the car and the road. Regarding whether such a learning process can work or not, on page 5, we mention that "we use neural networks for modeling ψ and verify that neural networks can indeed learn to infer the context, as shown in Table 1 in Appendix B.2"

On page 6, we mention that "The context encoder ψ encodes the last k interactions (denoted as H1) into a context encoding c1 := ψ(H1) The observation and context encodings are concatenated and fed to the policy to get the action.

content.comment:
> Section 6. In the experiments section, I am missing a description of the non stationarity setup and how the Zeus algorithm is dealing with non stationarity.

Thank you for the question. We model nonstationarity as a changing context over a family of stationary MDPs. During testing, the agent is evaluated on multiple held out environments (each with a different context) where the context is not accessible to the agent. In Figure 3 and 4, the x-axis denotes the number of steps in the training environments and movement along the x-axis can be seen as progression of training. At a fixed frequency, we take the trained model, and evaluate it on the heldout environments (in a zero-shot manner). The y-axis is showing the performance on these heldout environments. 

> If this is the main point in the paper then I would like to understand it exactly. I learn very little from the comparison to the baselines, this seems like an independent contribution. Instead I would like to see some connection to the theory part, and ablations, that explain me what are the important components of the algorithm and how sensitive they are to the non stationarity.

Thank you for the question. The key ingredient in our approach is the use of the context loss. In all the experiments, we include an ablation baseline where the agent is trained without using the context loss (as formulated by us). The other baselines consider other ways of inferring and leveraging the context. Comparisons with these baselines show how effectively does our approach leverages the context. These results are covered in figure 3 and 4. In figure 5, we show that the context representation constructed by ZeUS contains meaningful information about the true context of the BC-MDP.

We hope we have addressed all the questions reviewer had and look forward to address any other comments they may have!

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors study the problem of continual learning in RL. The paper is concerned with the problem of contextual block MDP. In this setting, an agent interacts with a stationary MDP for a while and the MDP changes once in a while. The authors also assume that the MDP has some rich state structure where a rich state can be mapped to a smaller state.

The paper proposes a deep learning method that has two main structures, 1) an encoder which given H time step of agent-environment interactions infers the context of the environment 2) and an encoder that maps rich observation to the smaller state. The outcome of the context encoder and observation encoder are then fed to the policy model to generate an action.
content.main_review:
The paper is well-motivated but the authors might find it useful to explain their algorithm in more depth in the main text. It is not that clear what is the algorithm. The authors provided a very high-level and abstract explanation but were not sufficient. The authors also need to motivate their assumptions. Also, they need to make a connection between their empirical approach and their theoretical statements.

--- A few points that the authors might be able to directly address during the rebuttal phase: 
1- In definition 4, do the authors prove that d_task is indeed a distance? If not, the authors are encouraged to provide proof. 
2- In Theorem 2, what does it mean that an algorithm to be Lipchitz? the authors are encouraged to provide a definition. 
3- After equation 2, what does "stopped gradient: mean?

4- Well written
-- Further concerns and suggestions: 
5- After reading the main part of the paper, it is still not clear how the learning works and how the learned algorithm works. 
5a- It seems, there is an encoder from experiences to context, and an encoder from rich observation to a state. Then a policy network uses these to produce an action. This is very abstract. A more detailed explanation is useful for how all these pieces and steps exactly happen. 
5b- How does the learning happen? what is the training algorithm? It seems there is a model/dynamics learning component that is not discussed in the main text. 
5c- "transition dynamics model and a reward model (via supervised learning)" how does this step happen? how the probability of the next state given the current state and action is learned? it is not discussed at all. 
6- It is not clear how valid are some of the assumptions. For example, assumption 1 is quite strong. Please motivate it.
7- A high-level comment, the authors' don't need to reply to it, but the theory in this paper seems a bit disconnected, it is quite challenging to see how to put the statements together and build a unified understanding. What do the results tell me? 
8- Following this line "These learned models allow us to construct a new MDP that is εR, εT , εc-close to the original" how the supervised learning happens not knowing the context? The algorithm seems to need the learned dynamic model to learn the context encoder, but identifying a context seems to be needed to learn the dynamics to begin with. Probably I am missing something. 
9- It seems rho does not show up in theorem 2, it seems a bit odd. Should the result depend on rho? 
10- The experiment study seems to do not advocate outstanding superior performance. 
11- When does the MDP change? how the algorithm infers any change?

I may have been wrong in the above statements.

content.title: Thank you for your feedback! 1/3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their detailed feedback and are glad that they find the paper "well-motivated". We address their questions below and look forward to discussing these points with them.

> The authors provided a very high-level and abstract explanation but were not sufficient.

We describe the implementation details, along with pseudo code in the appendix (section B). We will move some of the content to the main paper so that the paper contains main details.

> In definition 4, do the authors prove that d_task is indeed a distance? If not, the authors are encouraged to provide proof. 

We can show that d_task is a pseudometric as it is always >= 0, d(c_1,c_2) = d(c_2,c_1), d(c,c) = 0, and it is simple to see that it obeys the triangle inequality, i.e. that d(c_1,c_3) <= d(c_1,c_2) + d(c_2,c_3).

> In Theorem 2, what does it mean that an algorithm to be Lipchitz? the authors are encouraged to provide a definition. 

We have clarified the wording to be “If the testing error given the output of a learning algorithm is Lipschitz continuous…” which we have added a definition for and is also given as Example 4 in Robustness and Generalization, Xu & Mannor (2010), where it is discussed that feed-forward neural networks qualify. 

> After equation 2, what does "stopped gradient: mean?

"Stopped gradient" means that the gradients (corresponding to particular loss components) are not back propagated through the specific model components. For example, when we say that we stop the gradients for $\phi(o^{c_1}_{t+1}$ when computing the dynamics loss, it essentially means that we treat the $\phi(o^{c_1}_{t+1}$ term as a target for training the dynamics model. 

> 5- After reading the main part of the paper, it is still not clear how the learning works and how the learned algorithm works. 

We describe the implementation details, along with pseudo code in the appendix (section B). We will move some of the content to the main paper. We also include these details in our reply here (for the sake of completeness)

> 5a- It seems, there is an encoder from experiences to context, and an encoder from rich observation to a state. Then a policy network uses these to produce an action. This is very abstract. A more detailed explanation is useful for how all these pieces and steps exactly happen. 5b- How does the learning happen? what is the training algorithm? 

We describe the architecture of ZeUS in \cref{fig:main}. We have an observation encoder $\phi$ that encodes the pixel-observations into real-valued vectors. A buffer of interaction-history is maintained for computing the context. The context encoder first encodes the individual state-action transition pairs and then aggregates the representations using standard operations: \textit{sum}, \textit{mean}, \textit{concate}, \textit{product}, \textit{min} and \textit{max} \footnote{We experiment with these aggregation operators for all the baselines and not just ZeUS.}. All the components are instantiated using feedforward networks. During inference, assume that the agent is operating in some environment denoted by (latent) context $c_1$. At time $t$, the agent gets an observation $o_t^{c_1}$ which is encoded into $s_t^{c_1}:=\phi(o_t^{c_1})$\footnote{We overload notation here since the true state space is latent.}. The context encoder $\psi$ encodes the last $k$ interactions (denoted as $H_1$) into a context encoding $c_1:=\psi(H_1)$\footnote{We again overload notation here since the true context space is also latent.}. The observation and context encodings are concatenated and fed to the policy to get the action. 

During training, we sample a batch of interaction sequences from the buffer. For sake of exposition, we assume that we sample only 2 sequences $H_1$ and $H_2$. Similar to the inference pipeline, we compute $\phi(o_t^{c_1}), \psi(H_1), \phi(o_t^{c_2})$ and $\psi(H_2)$ and the loss (\cref{eq:total_loss}). We highlight that the algorithm does not know if the two (sampled) interactions correspond to the same context or not. Hence, in a small percentage of cases, $H_1$ and $H_2$ could correspond to the same context and the context loss will be equal to $0$. For implementing the loss in equation \cref{eq:total_loss}, we do not need access to the true context as the distance between the contexts can be approximated using the learned transition and reward models using \cref{def:smoothness}. The pseudo-code is provided in \cref{alg:algorithm} (\cref{appendix:implementation_details}). Since ZeUS is a representation learning algorithm, it must be paired with a policy optimization algorithm for end-to-end training. In the scope of this work, we use Soft Actor-Critic with auto-encoder loss (SAC-AE, \cite{yarats2019improving}), though ZeUS can be used with any policy optimization algorithm.

content.title: Thank you for your feedback 2/3
content.comment:
> 5c- "transition dynamics model and a reward model (via supervised learning)" how does this step happen? how the probability of the next state given the current state and action is learned? it is not discussed at all.

We mention the use of a dynamics model and a reward model (page 6, 3rd paragraph) and provide reference to the algorithm using these models (algorithm 2 in the appendix). We will move this detail to the main paper. Learning a transition model and a reward model is fairly standard in RL and is achieved via the dynamics loss and the reward loss respectively (eq 2). Specifically, the dynamics model takes as input the current state encoding (obtained using the observation encoder and denoted as o^{c_1}_t),  action and the context (obtained using the context encoder and denoted as \psi(H_1)). It  predicts the state encoding corresponding to the next observation. The ground truth (for training the transition model) is the encoding of the next observation that the agent actually observed (denoted as \phi(o^{c_1}_{t+1}). A similar process follows for the reward model where the observed reward acts as the ground truth. We will add this description to the paper.

> 6- It is not clear how valid are some of the assumptions. For example, assumption 1 is quite strong. Please motivate it. 

Assumption 1 is implicit in all the works that leverage neural networks to infer the context or to identify system parameters. Several examples are mentioned in the related work section and used as the baselines. In our work, we make this assumption explicit to ensure that the readers are aware of the underlying assumptions. In Table 1 (in appendix), we show that this assumptions holds well in practice.

> A high-level comment, the authors' don't need to reply to it, but the theory in this paper seems a bit disconnected, it is quite challenging to see how to put the statements together and build a unified understanding. What do the results tell me? 

The results say that if we have a Lipschitz BC-MDP, we can apply bounds for the ability of a learned policy to zero-shot generalize to new contexts from that MDP family. Furthermore, it is possible to do so with non-iid sampled data, as is often the case in reinforcement learning. However, many RL environments are known to be not Lipschitz. We provide a way to learn a Lipschitz context space (which gives us a Lipschitz BC-MDP) and modify the existing generalization bound to include the approximation error from the learned mapping of the ground truth, possibly non-Lipschitz BC-MDP to the Lipschitz one

> Following this line "These learned models allow us to construct a new MDP that is εR, εT , εc-close to the original" how the supervised learning happens not knowing the context? 

The context space is constructed using the context loss, but the objectives for learning the dynamics and reward models are stationary and defined. 

> The algorithm seems to need the learned dynamic model to learn the context encoder, but identifying a context seems to be needed to learn the dynamics to begin with. Probably I am missing something. 

The context encoder is trained via two loss components : (i) the dynamics + reward loss and (ii) the context loss (which incentivizes the context to be lipschitz). We think that the reviewer's question arises because we use the word context loss for one component in equation 2 which might give the impression that only that term is used for training the context.  We thank the reviewer for highlighting this and will reword it in the paper to avoid this confusion.

> It seems rho does not show up in theorem 2, it seems a bit odd. Should the result depend on rho? 

No it does not depend on rho. We point the reviewer to the result and proof for Theorem 10 in Xu & Mannor, 2010. 


> The experiment study seems to do not advocate outstanding superior performance.

Thank you for raising this point. We highlight some important aspects of the results: (i) In Figure 3, the baseline that is closest to our model is HyperDynamics (3 out of 4 cases). HyperDynamics is a memory and compute intensive baseline. As described in appendix (page 17, under "compute resources"), HyperDynamics needs a 32 GB gpu to run (other baselines are run on 16 GB gpus) and takes 1.4 times longer for training (for the same number of steps). Despite having a much smaller memory footprint and a much smaller runtime, our model consistently outperforms HyperDynamics (and the other baselines). In figure 4, the gap in performance values may look small but do consider that the range of rewards is also much smaller in these experiments. In figure 6, we show that as we get further away from the "seen" context distribution, our model degrades much more gracefully as compared to the other models.

Thank you for the question. We model nonstationarity as a changing context over a family of stationary MDPs. display_title: Official Review of Paper4654 by Reviewer coxs

content.summary_of_the_paper:
To study continual learning in non-stationary environments, the authors
propose modeling the problem as a block contextual Markov decision
process. The paper proposes a representation learning algorithm that
uses the lipschitz property to allow generalization to unseen MDPs
(through latent contexts). The proposed algorithm (ZeUS), is evaluated
on interpolation and extrapolation in various environments. The authors
find that ZeUS is better than similar system identification algorithms
and learns a structured context space.
content.main_review:
Strengths
---------

-   Experimental results, especially those in Figure 3, seem strongly in
    favor of the proposed algorithm (ZeUS). The error bars are
    surprisingly small, and so there is a large statistically
    significant difference in the performance increase. It is also good
    to see that the context space is more structured when including the
    context loss.

-   The theoretical results seem correct and useful, (but I have
    detailed some concerns below). Knowing that there is a performance
    guarantee for sufficiently similar contexts is good, and shows the
    continuing promise of lipschitz continuity as an enforceable
    property in RL algorithms.

Weaknesses
----------

-   The paper is not well positioned relative to other algorithms /
    baselines. There is a large literature that this paper draws on:
    contextual MDP, contextual decision processes, continual learning,
    meta-learning, system identification, etc. Some of these do not seem
    particularly relevant, such as the inclusion of a contextual
    observation per state (which i detail below). Taken together, it is
    difficult to discern the overall significance of the presented work.

-   While the theoretical results in section 4 are comprehensive, there
    is little insight and connection between the theory and the rest of
    the paper. For example, the context distance term is approximated in
    an unclear way. The loss being optimized bears only little
    resemblance to the task distance in the definition. These issues add
    up to call into question the contribution and importance of the
    algorithm's theoretical underpinning.

Detailed Comments
-----------------

-   Foot note page 2: This does not seem like an advantage without
    further qualification. Of course there is no forgetting when there
    is also no learning, but this can be said of any model that does not
    perform parameter updates. What is important is that the model is
    able to adapt even without parameter updates. While you state that
    this is the case, it does not communicate why or how this is
    achieved.

-   "Further, our model can be verified after training… We do not
    perform this type of formal verification, as current verification
    methods on neural networks only work for very small models, and are
    expensive to run"

    I do not understand what is being said here. Can the model be
    verified or not? Is this an advantage if it cannot be realistically
    done?

-   Definition 2: What is the difference between the shared observation
    space $\mathcal{O}$ and the context observation space
    $\mathcal{O}^c$?

-   Section 2: Block MDP is not a relaxation of a contextual markov
    decision processes (CMDP), which provides a context for an MDP
    episode. Block MDPs are relaxations of contextual decision processes
    (CDP), which provide per-state contexts. The naming is confusing,
    but these are very different ideas.

-   Page 4 robot example: the observation space is the same and
    specified by the camera that the robot uses.

-   "Note that Definition 3 is not a limiting assumption because we do
    not assume access to the context variables c1 and c2, and they can
    therefore be chosen so that the Lipschitz condition is always
    satisfied. In this work, we focus on a method for learning a context
    space that satisfies the above property."

    Although the true underlying context is not available, it does not
    seem correct to say that the c_1 and c_2 can be arbitrarily chosen
    to satisfy definition 3, as these contexts are also used in the dynamics
    model. There may be degenerate solutions that satisfy the definition.

-   Section 4, Paragraph 1: Why is it that the results to hold true for
    any state or observation space? If this is the case, what is the
    need for the BC-MDP formalism introduced in the previous section?

-   Section 4, Assumption 1: I think there is a third assumption
    implicit here. The transitions are determined by a policy, and
    identification can depend on the policy. Hence, shouldn't there be
    an exploration requirement as well? This is partially addressed by
    definition 5 for theorem 2, but exploration (or some policy
    dependence) should still be necessary for identifiability.

-   Section 5, Equation 2: Context 2 only appears in the first term
    (context-loss). Shouldn't the dynamics and reward terms have
    additional terms that optimize the reward / dynamics with respect to
    context 2?

-   Section 5: "Specifically, we train a transition dynamics model and a
    reward model (via supervised learning) and use their output to
    approximate d(c1, c2)."

    It is not at all clear how this distance is estimated using either
    definition 3 or 4. Do you use the learned models to approximate the
    individual distances across contexts and then add them? If so, there
    are many sources of error: the approximation error of the models,
    the sampling procedure (which approximates the max), the inner
    optimization of the wasserstein loss, etc. Definition 3 is also
    scaled by unknown constants and the bound most hold uniformly over
    all state-action pairs. It is not clear that such a noisy target
    would be helpful for learning with Equation 2.

-   Section 5, ZeUS Architecture: I understand that the assumptions of
    identifiability in Section 4 use just the last k transitions. Since
    the implementation differs from the assumptions, I wonder why the
    context encoder still only looks at k transitions? Why not the
    entire trajectory?

-   Section 6, Figure 3: Are the transition dynamics changing in each
    plot? For example, is the cheetah torso changing every X number of
    environment steps? Where does this occur on the x-axis? I am
    surprised to see relatively monotonic improvement during training,
    given that there are parameter updates during training on different
    tasks (and hence, catastrophic forgetting can occur during
    training).

-   Section 6, Figure 4: Although the reward is bounded, I think that
    aggregating different reward functions in one return plot is not
    necessarily correct. One reward function could be harder to learn
    and hence the return will be overall lower than another "easier"
    reward function.

-   Section 6, Figure 5: From these plots, it does seem that the context
    loss does lead to more structure. However, it is puzzling that the
    largest differences aren't between the smallest and largest index,
    but between interior tasks (such as between 6 and 4 in the left
    plot). Task index 7 in general has relatively lower pairwise
    differences compared to other indicies.

Minor Comments
--------------

-   Page 3: T environment's -\> The environment's
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper proposes a novel representation learning architecture for the
problem of learning from a sequence of MDPs, but there are a number
issues that hold the paper back. The theory, while welcome, is
disconnected from the proposed algorithm on a number of levels and does
provide much overall insight into the problem of generalization to
unseen contexts. There are a number of design decisions in the actual
algorithm that are unjustified or confusing. I have detailed all these
in the "Detailed Comments" section. My decision, therefore, is to lean
towards rejection.

content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their detailed feedback and are glad that they find "Experimental results, especially those in Figure 3, seem strongly in favor of the proposed algorithm (ZeUS)". We address their questions below and look forward to discussing these points with them.

>Foot note page 2: This does not seem like an advantage without further qualification. Of course there is no forgetting when there is also no learning, but this can be said of any model that does not perform parameter updates. What is important is that the model is able to adapt even without parameter updates. While you state that this is the case, it does not communicate why or how this is achieved.

Thank you for raising this important point. The model adapts by inferring the correct context and passing that context as input to the policy. None of the model parameters are updated in the process.

> I do not understand what is being said here. Can the model be verified or not? Is this an advantage if it cannot be realistically done?

Thank you for this question. The model can be verified in the sense that algorithms for verification exist. However, these methods do not yet scale for large models, making them quite expensive to run. Whether the verification can be done "realistically" depends on the size of the model. Nevertheless, it is advantageous to have models that can be verified. For our setup, the model will stay true to the verification since the agent’s parameters are not updated when adapted to the unseen environments. 

> Definition 2: What is the difference between the shared observation space O and the context observation space Oc?

Consider the example of a robot operating in different warehouses. In one warehouse, it only observes/interacts with solid objects like metallic cubes and in another warehouse, it only observes/interacts with deformable objects like clothes. The shared observation space is the space of all the objects (solid + deformable) while the context observation space is the space of solid or deformable objects. We will make this distinction more explicit in the paper.


> Section 2: Block MDP is not a relaxation of a contextual markov decision processes (CMDP), which provides a context for an MDP episode. Block MDPs are relaxations of contextual decision processes (CDP), which provide per-state contexts. The naming is confusing, but these are very different ideas.

You are correct. We have checked the writing in Section 3 and believe there is some confusion about what we wrote. To clarify, we do not claim that block MDPs are relaxations of CMDPs. We are combining block MDP assumptions with those of CMDPs to handle settings where the observation space can change across different contexts. We will update the paper to get rid of this ambiguity.

>Although the true underlying context is not available, it does not seem correct to say that the c_1 and c_2 can be arbitrarily chosen to satisfy definition 3, as these contexts are also used in the dynamics model. There may be degenerate solutions that satisfy the definition.

We are learning a context space such that c_1 and c_2 are close with respect to some distance metric (like L2)  if their corresponding MDPs have dynamics that are close. Therefore, the dynamics model will be Lipschitz with respect to L2 metric in context space.

> Section 4, Paragraph 1: Why is it that the results to hold true for any state or observation space? If this is the case, what is the need for the BC-MDP formalism introduced in the previous section?

The result that holds true for any state or observation space is that "Lipschitz property aids generalization". We need the BC-MDP formalism to design an algorithm that can leverage this result and perform online inference of “unknown unknowns” to solve a family of tasks 

> Section 4, Assumption 1: I think there is a third assumption implicit here. The transitions are determined by a policy, and identification can depend on the policy. Hence, shouldn't there be an exploration requirement as well? This is partially addressed by definition 5 for theorem 2, but exploration (or some policy dependence) should still be necessary for identifiability.

Thank you for raising this subtle point. Transitions do depend on the policy but exploration may not be a necessary requirement for inferring the context. However, we do agree with the general importance of exploration when training an RL agent and will include this point in the paper. We will also reword the first assumption to include the role of the policy as well. 
 
> Section 5, Equation 2: Context 2 only appears in the first term (context-loss). Shouldn't the dynamics and reward terms have additional terms that optimize the reward / dynamics with respect to context 2?

Thank you for this point. There should be additional terms corresponding to the reward/dynamics loss for context 2
